results.text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 56 Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major energy supply shock in 2026. to 8.3 percent between January and June, with higher inflation expectations for 2026. Energy prices have increased, as well, by 1.1 percentage points between January and June 2026 (excluding China). question: How did inflation expectations change among market participants following the February 2026 conflict?

gold.evidence: Among market participants, inflation expectations for 2026 have also risen, from 2.7 percent according to preconflict February surveys to 3.4 percent in July.

results.text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 56 Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major energy supply shock in 2026. The conflict in the Middle East involving major energy producers, which began at the end of February 2026, has caused a surge in headline inflation in these countries, to 3.6 percent in June 2026, from the preconflict level of 2.6 percent (figure 2.4). Among market participants, inflation expectations for 2026 have also risen, from 2.7 percent according to preconflict February surveys to 3.4 percent in July. Excluding China, which has been relatively insulated from the shock, partly because of its large petroleum reserves, inflation in commodity-importing LMICs increased from 7.0 percent

to 8.3 percent between January and June, with higher inflation expectations for 2026. Energy prices have increased, as well, by 1.1 percentage points between January and June 2026 (excluding China). To ease price pressures, several central banks have raised interest rates. In addition, several commodityimporting LMICs have introduced subsidies in response to higher fuel prices (World Bank 2026b). question: How did domestic banks exposure to sovereign assets in IDA countries compare to banks in IBRD countries?

gold.evidence: domestic banks in IDA countries have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than banks in IBRD countries have

results.text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 66 Domestic creditors in both IDA and International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) countries have elevated their exposure to the sovereign over the past 20 years. This move mirrors their respective governments’ growing reliance on domestic financing. However, domestic banks in IDA countries have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than banks in IBRD countries have (figure 2.11). This higher exposure reflects less developed and less diversified private sectors in many IDA countries, as well as fewer investment options as compared to IBRD markets.
